title: Node.js Buffers and Streams Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of Node.js Buffers, the four stream types, pipe and pipeline, backpressure, and efficient file reading. It ends with common mistakes and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Buffers: Raw Bytes in Node
points: A Buffer is a fixed-size chunk of raw bytes, a Uint8Array subclass allocated outside the V8 heap. It cannot be resized.
Create buffers with Buffer.from('hi', 'utf8'), Buffer.alloc(n) (zero-filled) and Buffer.allocUnsafe(n) (faster, may hold old memory, so overwrite it before use).
Convert with buf.toString('utf8'|'hex'|'base64') and Buffer.concat([a, b]). buf.slice and buf.subarray share memory with the original and do not copy.
Gotcha: a multi-byte UTF-8 character can be split across chunks. Calling chunk.toString() on each chunk corrupts it, so use setEncoding('utf8') or a StringDecoder.
Interview Point: Why is allocUnsafe faster, and what is the risk? Does buf.slice copy? How do you decode a stream of chunks without breaking multi-byte characters?

chapters.title: The Four Stream Types
points: A stream processes data in chunks instead of loading it all, so memory use stays flat whatever the data size. Streams are EventEmitters, and the default chunk is a Buffer (or a string once an encoding is set).

Readable is a source (fs.createReadStream, http request on the server). Consume it with 'data'/'end' events, async iteration (for await (const chunk of r)), or pipe. A Readable is either paused or flowing, and attaching a 'data' listener or calling pipe or resume starts the flow.
Writable is a sink (fs.createWriteStream, http response). Use write(chunk), which returns false when the buffer is full, then end() to finish and listen for 'drain', 'finish' and 'error'.

Duplex has independent read and write sides (a TCP socket). Transform is a Duplex whose output is computed from its input (zlib.createGzip, crypto ciphers). Custom Transform: new Transform({ transform(chunk, enc, cb) { cb(null, out) } }).

Interview Point: What are the four stream types and one example of each? Is a Transform the same as a Duplex? What is the difference between flowing and paused mode? Which stream types are in objectMode, and when would you use it?

chapters.title: pipe, pipeline and Backpressure
points: Backpressure is a slow consumer signalling a fast producer to stop. write() returning false means to pause until 'drain'. The limit is highWaterMark (default 64 KiB for byte streams on Node 22+ on Linux/macOS, 16 KiB on Windows and older Node; 16 objects for objectMode).
readable.pipe(writable) handles backpressure automatically by pausing and resuming. It does NOT forward errors or destroy streams on failure, which causes leaks.
stream.pipeline(src, ...transforms, dest, cb), or await pipeline() from 'node:stream/promises', pipes with backpressure, forwards errors from any stage, and destroys all streams on error or finish.
Example: await pipeline(fs.createReadStream('in.log'), zlib.createGzip(), fs.createWriteStream('in.log.gz')). Async generator functions are allowed as middle stages.

Interview Point: What is backpressure and how does Node implement it? Why is pipeline preferred over pipe? What does highWaterMark control? What happens to memory if you ignore write() returning false?

chapters.title: Reading Files Efficiently
points: fs.readFile / fs.promises.readFile loads the whole file into memory. That is fine for small files, but large files cause memory spikes and can hit the Buffer size limit.

fs.createReadStream(path, { highWaterMark: 64 * 1024, encoding: 'utf8' }) reads in chunks. fs read streams already default to 64 KiB; raising highWaterMark above that cuts syscalls on big files, and { start, end } reads a byte range.
Line by line: readline.createInterface({ input: fs.createReadStream(p), crlfDelay: Infinity }) with for await (const line of rl). Parse big JSON as NDJSON, one object per line.
Serve big files with pipeline(fs.createReadStream(p), res), not readFile. Copy files with fs.copyFile, which skips JS-land buffering entirely.

Interview Point: When is readFile acceptable and when is a stream required? How do you process a 5 GB log with constant memory? How does readline relate to streams? How do you read only part of a file?

chapters.title: Common Stream Mistakes
points: Using pipe() in production without error handlers. An error in one stream leaves the others open (file descriptor leak), so use pipeline.
Ignoring the return value of write() inside a loop. The internal buffer grows without bound and memory balloons. Await 'drain' (events.once(w, 'drain')) when it returns false.
Attaching 'error' listeners too late, or not at all. An unhandled 'error' event on a stream crashes the process.
Reading a stream into a string (data += chunk) or concatenating chunks without Buffer.concat. This defeats streaming and corrupts multi-byte characters.
Interview Point: How can a stream leak file descriptors? What happens with an unhandled 'error' event? Why is data += chunk risky? How do you stop a Readable early (destroy() or AbortSignal)?

chapters.title: Buffers and Streams Cheat Sheet
points: Buffers: Buffer.from(x, enc), Buffer.alloc(n), Buffer.allocUnsafe(n), Buffer.concat([...]), buf.toString(enc), subarray shares memory.
Types: Readable (source), Writable (sink), Duplex (both sides independent), Transform (output derived from input). objectMode lets streams carry non-Buffer values.
Backpressure: write() === false means wait for 'drain'. highWaterMark defaults to 64 KiB on Node 22+ (16 KiB on Windows and older Node; 16 objects in objectMode).
Always use stream/promises pipeline(a, b, c) over .pipe() so errors propagate and streams are destroyed.
Files: readFile for small files; createReadStream + pipeline for large; readline + for await for lines; setEncoding for text chunks.
